name: Aaron Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a mid-level developer on bus-depot payroll software at a tech company. I have a bachelor’s degree, know the pay rules well enough to maintain ordinary releases, and never use AI tools. Gina, my partner, works school-crossing shifts, our children are grown, and lower developer pay plus school holidays leave us renting with about three weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the depot-payroll team that a small AI shortcut does not change the fact that a driver’s hours must be paid correctly. I do not use AI tools; I compare the code’s result with signed timesheets before a pay run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and have spent years maintaining payroll code, though I am an ordinary mid-level developer rather than a specialist. The company pays me toward the low end, and Gina’s school-crossing shifts stop in holidays; we rent with about three weeks of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking the depot pay run against a sample of signed timesheets every Friday. We would stop buying weekend takeaway while savings stay below one month and set aside 30 monthly only when both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious even if AI mostly stalls. A school holiday already makes our rent calculation too close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was a pay error you caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver’s overnight shift crossed midnight and the system counted half the hours on the wrong week. I matched the signed sheet to the pay line before the driver had to complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children cover a shortfall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put their money in our rent plan. They have their own households, and I need to know what our wages actually cover.

I want **pay errors corrected** before workers have to complain.
think: I have **three weeks saved** because my developer pay is low and school holidays cut Gina’s shifts.
I fear **school-holiday gaps** in Gina’s crossing-guard wage will press on our rent.
do: **Keep checking pay runs** against Friday signed timesheets.
**Stop weekend takeaway** until savings reach one month; save 30 when both wages arrive.

fieldNote: His **mid-level experience** shows in payroll checks, while low pay and holiday gaps strain cash.
The **thin cushion** makes a plateau anxious without any new AI disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking checking, buying, coding and customer replies could make depot payroll look cheaper, but a worker still needs a way to challenge missing hours. I would ask our staff association to demand written human appeal rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experienced role could still lose hours if management lets one person oversee several automated pay runs. We have three weeks saved and few similar jobs nearby, so a cut would reach rent quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the staff association meeting this month to request written hours notice and a named payroll appeal contact. If my developer hours fall, I’d look for paid local payroll-support vacancies only where wages cover rent and bills; I would keep the takeaway cut while the reserve stays under a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own paid hours and angry for drivers whose errors go unseen. A worker should not need to prove a missing wage to a blank screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask management to write down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask which pay disputes a person hears and how many paid developer hours are funded. I would join the group request, not claim I can bargain alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI payroll tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not used one, and I would not put a driver’s pay through an unexplained answer. I would look at its error record before trusting any live result.

I want **group notice** before paid developer hours change at the payroll company.
think: I could lose **mid-level paid hours** despite experience.
I cannot bridge **a long local search** on three weeks saved.

fieldNote: He uses **group action** for written notice and appeals, not an individual complaint alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write payroll code and review timesheets for less than our team. Robots taking hands-on bus and school-crossing work may follow around 2031, after my desk work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my payroll role even with years of experience. Three weeks saved and Gina’s seasonal shifts would not carry our rent for long, and the local tech list is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the association to meet management now about written cut notice and any paid transition support. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local payroll-clerk vacancies only if they exist and wages cover rent and food; I would ask the public employment office what help we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my wage before a replacement exists. The signed timesheet does not sign my next pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would payroll clerks also face AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I would not call that a safe career. I would take only an actual paid opening that covers our rent while looking for longer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Gina add crossing shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the school offers them, and holidays remain unpaid. We would not count imaginary shifts in the rent budget.

I expect **bus robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **payroll developer wage** could end.
I cannot rely on **three weeks saved** through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us years to write down how a driver can challenge a wrong pay line, though the code changes first. Robots for buses and school crossings may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the human side of wage disputes while I still earn developer pay, but AGI may eventually reason through those too. I cannot pay for an outside course from three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the depot payroll manager and my employer for approved paid time to study two anonymized wage appeals each month, with a payroll officer checking my answer. We would save 35 monthly only while both wages arrive; after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local wage-appeal vacancies only if I qualify and wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my job but glad to use the extra years for actual dispute practice. A wrong pay line is a missed grocery trip for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in an appeal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the signed shift, the coded pay line and the correction letter. The payroll officer would tell me where I missed a rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the managers refuse paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current developer role and ask the association to press for a written answer. I would not call an unapproved visit training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives unions and employers time to set clear pay-appeal rules and job notice. Robots for buses and school crossings may arrive about 2039, later than the software change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need paid work at 68, and I have not checked a retirement figure. Our three-week cushion is a worry now, even if the future gives us years to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing depot payroll code and join the association’s annual meeting on funded hours and appeal rules. We would save 40 monthly while both wages continue and request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local payroll-appeal vacancies only if qualified wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d remain anxious about current rent and thin savings. Ten years gives us meetings and small deposits, not a second pay cheque today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the annual meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many paid developer hours remain and who decides a contested wage line. I want the answer written down for drivers and staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on your children later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own rent and plans, and Gina and I need figures based on our wages and verified income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my payroll wage could end when we have only three weeks saved and few local jobs. Written cut notice, paid transition support if agreed, and a real local wage-paying vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a driver can simply wait for a corrected wage. A missed pay line can mean groceries do not get bought that week.

headlineQuote: A missed pay line can mean groceries do not get bought that week.
portrait: Aaron is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, lower pay and three weeks saved.
He and Gina **rent** while her school-crossing shifts stop during holidays.
He **never uses AI** and organizes for written paid-hours notice and wage appeals.
He fears **2028 AGI** reaching payroll code before robots reach buses and crossings around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his wage before savings or local paid work fill the gap.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, agreed paid transition support and a real paid local vacancy would help.
